CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Cooking — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the cooking club habit: the child wears the apron and makes the choices, the grown-up owns the heat, and one simple dish becomes the family’s Tuesday classic.

What is this?

Cooking club is regular kitchen time with real jobs — pouring, stirring, spreading, tearing — where the printed skills are Food & Independence: knowing what goes into food and making some of it yourself.

What does it mean?

Cooking is the most useful math and science lab in the house: measuring is fractions, cooking is chemistry, and eating the result is the best feedback loop ever designed. Choosing the menu trains decision-making with immediate, delicious consequences.

What does the child need to know?

A stable chair or learning tower, one mixing bowl, child-safe tools (a butter knife genuinely cuts a banana), ingredients for one simple dish, and a hand-wash station. Heat stays with the grown-up.

Why this matters

Children who cook eat braver — they try what they made. Kitchen jobs also build sequencing, measuring, patience while things bake, and the pride of feeding the family.

What it teaches

Sequencing and following steps, measuring and counting, hand strength (stirring thick batter is a workout), kitchen safety habits, and tasting vocabulary (salty, sour, crunchy).

Words to learn

chefrecipemixstirpourmeasurebaketasteingredient

Say this to your child

“"Cooking club is open — tonight YOU are the chef and I am your helper. Wash those hands, chef! First we read the recipe. Which ingredient goes in first?"”

Step by step

  1. Wash hands and tie the apron — the uniform makes it official.
  2. Read the recipe out loud and count the ingredients together.
  3. Assign the child the safe jobs: measuring, pouring, stirring, arranging.
  4. Chef decides: more cheese or less? round shapes or stars? The helper executes.
  5. Taste test at the end with real words — what is salty, what is sweet — then the chef signs off the dish with a name.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the cook’s whisk stands tall in a big bowl with the apron already on — the whisk and apron are the two tools that say this kitchen belongs to the chef today.

Ask your child

"What does the chef do first?" (wash hands) "What is our helper’s job?" (the oven — heat is the grown-up’s) "What does our dish taste like?" "What should we cook next week?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may plate the dish like a restaurant, invent a dish name with its own song, or set a pretend menu for tomorrow — chefs with one success book the next night immediately.

Out in the real world

Chefs, bakers, food scientists and dietitians all started by stirring something at a counter beside a grown-up. Every restaurant was once a kitchen with a chair in it.

Try it together

Restaurant night: the child writes (or draws) the menu, takes the family’s orders with a notepad, and the family eats whatever the chef assembled. Tips are paid in bedtime stories.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who washes hands in cooking club?" (everybody, first) "Name your job tonight." (measure, pour, stir...) "What does the grown-up own?" (the heat and the oven)

This lesson pairs with the Cooking flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.
